What defines the motion? 📉🎢  ​In mechanics, the path an object takes depends entirely on the FORCE acting on it. ​🚀 Projectile Motion:  ​The Force: Constant (Gravity). ​The Path: A Parabola. ​Example: Kicking a football. ⚽  ​🕰️ Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM):  ​The Force: Variable (Proportional to displacement). ​The Path: Oscillation (Sine Wave over time). ​Example: A pendulum or a spring. 🌀  ​One creates a journey, the other creates a cycle. 🔄 ​💾 Save this post to remember the difference!  ​#sciencevisualized #physics #mechanics #kinematics #shm

The most important loop in Physics. 🔄📏  ​Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) happens when a force tries to bring an object back to its resting position (Equilibrium).  ​The Energy Cycle:  🔴 At the Extremes (Edges): Speed is Zero, but Potential Energy is Max. (The force is pulling hardest here!)  🟢 At the Center (Equilibrium): Potential Energy is Zero, but Speed is Max. (It zooms right past!)  ​This back-and-forth exchange is what creates the Sine Waves you see in your textbooks. 📉✍️  ​🚀 Follow ScienceVisualised for more mechanics simulations! 💾 Save this for your next Physics test.  ​#sciencevisualized #physics #mechanics #shm #pendulum

Beam or Spread? It depends on the size of the gap. 📏〰️  ​Diffraction is the bending of waves around obstacles or through openings. The video above shows the Golden Rule of Diffraction:  ​1️⃣ Wide Gap: When the opening is much larger than the wavelength, the wave passes through with barely any spreading. (It acts like a ray).  2️⃣ Narrow Gap: When the opening is close to the size of the wavelength, the wave spreads out in a perfect semi-circle! 📡 ​This is why 5G signals (short waves) get blocked easily, while radio waves (long waves) can wrap around mountains! 🏔️📻  ​🚀 Follow ScienceVisualised for more physics simulations! 💾 Save this to remember the difference!  ​#sciencevisualized #physics #engineering #telecom #diffraction waves stemeducation physicslovers visualscience tech

Why does light bend when it enters glass or water? 🔦📐  ​It’s all about speed. Light travels fastest in a vacuum. When it hits a denser medium (like water or glass), it hits the "brakes" and pivots. This bending is called Refraction.   ​This is why diamonds sparkle (high refractive index!) and why you have to aim below a fish to catch it. 💎🐟  ​🚀 Follow for more physics visualisations! 💾 Save this for your next optics exam.  ​#sciencevisualized #physics #stem #sciencefacts #refraction

What happens when two waves meet in the same space? 🌊➕🌊  ​They adhere to the Principle of Superposition, resulting in Interference.   There are two main types:  ​1️⃣ Constructive Interference: The crests line up. The waves combine to form a larger wave (Louder sound, brighter light).  2️⃣ Destructive Interference: A crest meets a trough. They cancel each other out (Silence, darkness).  ​From the colors on a soap bubble 🫧 to the dead spots in your room's acoustics, interference is everywhere!  ​🚀 Follow ScienceVisualised to see the unseen! 💾 Save this for your physics notes.  ​#sciencevisualized #physics #optics #sciencefacts #stem

How can a particle be in multiple states at once? ⚛️🌀  ​In classical physics, things are definite. A switch is On or Off. But in Quantum Mechanics, systems exist in a "Superposition"—a combination of all possible states simultaneously.   ​Think of it like music. 🎵 A single note is a state. But a chord is a superposition of multiple notes played together. ​It is only when we "observe" or measure the system that the Superposition collapses into a single, definite reality.
